after a previous service call. This is embarrassingly common and saves everyone time when checked
early. Field action: Reset breakers or overloads only after verifying the cause is resolved. Reseat loose connections. Report all findings. If the safety circuit is open, identify which device is tripped but do not bypass it. Escalate
to ThyssenKrupp for drive faults, contactor replacement, or unresolved electrical issues. Rope and Sheave Problems
All rope and sheave work is contractor work. Our field technicians perform visual inspections and report
findings, but never adjust, replace, or tension ropes. This section helps technicians identify problems and
provide accurate reports to ThyssenKrupp. 4
Hoist Rope Inspection
CSA B44 specifies the criteria for rope replacement. During visual inspections, check for:
• Broken wires. Count visible broken wires per rope lay (one complete twist of the strands around the
core). CSA B44 specifies the maximum number of broken wires per lay before replacement is required. Even a few broken wires should be documented and reported. See the Safety Code Quick Reference for
the specific numeric thresholds. • Diameter reduction. Measure rope diameter with calipers and compare to the original diameter (recorded
on the rope data tag or in the maintenance records). A reduction of more than a certain percentage from
the nominal diameter indicates internal wear and requires replacement. Ropes wear from the inside as
well as the outside. • Corrosion. Surface rust is common and not always critical, but extensive corrosion weakens the wire
strands. Look for pitting, flaking, or discoloration along the length of the rope. Corrosion is particularly
common in hoistways exposed to moisture (buildings with rooftop machine rooms, coastal environments,
or poor drainage). • Bird-caging. This occurs when the outer strands bulge outward from the rope core, usually caused by a
sudden release of tension. Bird-caging is a serious condition requiring immediate rope replacement. • Unequal tension. All hoist ropes in a set should carry approximately equal load.

Fire Service Test Records
Common violations: no record of Phase I and Phase II testing in the log book, expired testing records, and
incomplete records (only one phase tested). Fire service testing should be performed and documented during
routine maintenance visits per the maintenance contract schedule. Rope Wear
Wire rope deterioration beyond allowable limits triggers a fail and often leads to mandatory replacement. Indicators: broken wires exceeding the allowable count per rope lay, reduction in diameter indicating internal
wear, corrosion (particularly in humid environments), and uneven wear patterns suggesting sheave or
alignment problems. Ropes approaching their limits should be flagged for proactive replacement. Emergency Lighting
Emergency lighting must activate automatically when normal power is lost. Common failures: dead or weak
battery packs, burned-out bulbs, and non-functional transfer circuitry (goes unnoticed because normal
power is present). Test during every routine maintenance visit by briefly disconnecting the car lighting circuit. Device Type Considerations
Our fleet includes several device types, each affecting inspection scope and preparation:
• Passenger Elevators (~72% of our fleet): standard device type, follows the periodic inspection process
described above. • Freight Elevators (E-type and P-type): additional requirements for rated load, door configuration (often
vertical bi-parting), and industrial environment hazards (dust, chemical exposure, vibration). 13
• Observation Elevators: glass panels add inspection points for glass integrity, mounting security, and
hoistway visibility. Schindler handles most of these installations. • LULA Elevators (Limited Use/Limited Application): smaller, lower-speed devices for small buildings or
accessibility. Own subset of CSA B44 requirements; shorter inspections. • Sidewalk Elevators: vertical access between sidewalk and basement. Unique weather exposure and
security considerations. • Material Lifts (ATD), Power Type Manlifts, and Special Installations: specialized CSA B44 sections apply. Technicians must be familiar with the specific requirements. • Temporary Elevators: used during construction, licensed under temporary licenses, inspected as ED-
Inspection Temp Lic.

3. Rope condition. Inspect hoist ropes and governor ropes for displacement from sheave grooves, kinking,
or contact damage. Ropes that have jumped off sheaves require contractor re-seating. 4. Car frame alignment. Check for twisting, hoistway contact, or displaced components. 5. Machine room equipment. Check the drive machine, controller, and governor for displacement or
damage. Contact the appropriate contractor for a formal post-seismic inspection on any device where damage is
suspected. The elevator must not return to service until the contractor confirms it is safe. Equipment Failure Scenarios
This section covers the most serious equipment failure scenarios and the correct response for each. See the
Traction Elevator Troubleshooting Guide for diagnostic procedures and Common Failure Modes by Elevator
Type for failure patterns and fleet trends. Broken or Damaged Hoist Rope
Most traction elevators use multiple steel ropes (typically 3 to 8) in parallel, so a single rope failure does not
cause the car to fall. However, any rope failure is a critical safety event. If a hoist rope breaks during operation:
1. The governor should activate the car safety device, gripping the guide rails and stopping the car. 2. Treat this as an entrapment with a critical safety failure. Rescue passengers, then secure the device. 9
3. The device must not operate again until all ropes have been inspected and damaged ropes replaced. All
rope replacement is contractor work (ThyssenKrupp for traction systems). 4. Report to TSSA within 24 hours. A broken hoist rope is reportable regardless of injury. If rope damage is discovered during inspection:
1. Shut down the device immediately, regardless of how many ropes remain intact. Broken wires, corrosion,
or deformation in one rope indicates conditions that may affect others. 2. Contact ThyssenKrupp for a full rope inspection and replacement assessment. 3. Update the device status to "Out of Service" with the reason documented. Never operate an elevator with a known damaged rope, even if "most ropes are fine." Safety margins
assume all ropes are in good condition. Operating with damaged ropes invalidates those margins. Hydraulic System Failure
Hydraulic failures range from minor leaks to catastrophic events. The most serious is rapid oil loss (blowout),
where the car descends uncontrollably.

Use your power quality meter to verify voltage on all three phases. Field action: Check and reseat encoder connections. Report findings and escalate drive or sheave issues to
ThyssenKrupp. 3
Symptom: Excessive Vibration
Vibration felt in the machine room, transmitted through the ropes, or reported by passengers:
1. Check motor mounting bolts for looseness. Vibration can loosen mounting hardware over time, and a
loose motor amplifies vibration. 2. Listen to the bearings. Worn bearings produce vibration that increases with speed. 3. Inspect the sheave for uneven groove wear. A worn sheave causes ropes to seat unevenly, creating
vibration at the frequency of the sheave rotation. 4. For geared systems, check the gearbox for abnormal noise. Gear tooth wear or low lubricant levels cause
vibration and noise. Check the oil level and look for metal particles in the oil, which indicate gear wear. 5. Check the motor coupling (geared systems). A worn or misaligned coupling transmits vibration between
the motor and gearbox. Field action: Tighten any loose mounting hardware. All other causes require contractor diagnosis and repair. Symptom: Motor Won't Start
The elevator does not respond to hall calls. The car sits at a floor with doors closed and no movement:
1. Verify power supply to the motor and drive. Check all three phases at the disconnect. A blown fuse or
tripped breaker on one phase will prevent the motor from starting (or cause it to attempt to start on two
phases, which the drive should fault on). 2. Check the main contactor. The contactor connects power to the drive. If it is not pulling in, check the
control circuit that energizes the contactor coil. A failed contactor is a common cause of "dead elevator"
calls. 3. Check whether the overload has tripped. If so, investigate why before resetting (see Motor Overheating
above). 4. Check the drive for fault codes. Many drive faults will prevent the motor from starting. Record all fault
codes. 5. Verify the safety circuit is complete. An open safety circuit (any safety device in the chain is tripped) will
prevent the elevator from running. Check the safety circuit status on the controller. Common safety
devices that trip: governor switch, pit stop switch, car top stop switch, door interlocks, buffer switches.

• 6 months to 1 year: expands to cover most of a periodic inspection, since idle components may have
deteriorated. • Over 1 year: essentially an initial inspection. Ropes may have corroded, hydraulic seals may have dried
out, electrical connections may have corroded, and control systems may have developed faults. The Re-Activation Process
1. Complete all remediation work that prompted the shutdown (or maintenance required to bring the device
to operating condition). 2. Submit a re-activation request to the TSSA. 3. The TSSA schedules the re-activation inspection. 4. Prepare as for a periodic inspection, with attention to items that may have deteriorated during the
shutdown. 5. Pass the inspection. The device receives clearance to return to service. The device must not carry passengers or freight until the TSSA has issued clearance. This is non-negotiable,
regardless of pressure from the building owner. Other Inspection Types
The following inspection types appear less frequently in our records but are important to understand when
they occur. ED-Unscheduled Inspection
A TSSA-initiated inspection outside the regular periodic cycle. Unlike enforcement actions, these are not
necessarily triggered by a compliance concern. The TSSA may conduct them as part of targeted campaigns
(focusing on a device type or age range), random audits, or in response to industry-wide safety bulletins. ED-Sub Inspection and ED-Sub Inspection Major
Performed by inspectors subcontracted by the TSSA to handle volume during peak periods. Same standards
and procedures as TSSA staff inspectors. From our perspective, preparation and response are identical. ED-PWGSC Insp and ED-PWGSC Foll-Up
Inspections of elevating devices on federal government properties. PWGSC (Public Works and Government
Services Canada) properties are inspected by the TSSA under a federal service agreement. These follow CSA
B44 but may include additional federal requirements. The follow-up variant verifies resolution of issues from
the initial inspection. ED-Non-Mandated Insp ON and ED-Non-Mandated Followup ON
Voluntary inspections requested by a building owner or by us. Useful for independent assessment before a
modernization decision or after significant repair work. The follow-up variant tracks resolution of any issues
found.

Follow up
Some compliance orders from the previous inspection were resolved, but others remain outstanding, or the
inspector found that some corrections were inadequate. A subsequent follow-up inspection will be
scheduled. 11
Our action: Same as Fail, focused on the remaining open orders. Review what was accepted and what was
not. If a correction was rejected, determine why and redo the work. Track the next follow-up deadline. Shutdown
The inspector found severe violations presenting an immediate safety hazard. The device is ordered out of
service immediately. Can occur during any inspection type. Our action: This triggers the TSSA Shutdown Response procedure (see Emergency Response Protocols). Device is taken out of service immediately with "Out of Service" signage posted. Notify the building owner,
zone manager, and Compliance and Regulatory Affairs. Develop a remediation plan, complete the work,
submit a re-activation request, and pass the re-activation inspection before the device returns to service. Shutdowns are tracked as critical compliance events and reviewed by senior management. Unable to Inspect
The inspector could not complete the inspection. Common reasons: access denied, device not operational
(already shut down or under construction), unsafe conditions, or no qualified person available to operate the
elevator. Our action: Reschedule as soon as possible. Determine and correct the underlying cause (access
coordination failure, technician scheduling gap). Repeated "Unable to Inspect" results can trigger
enforcement action, which is a significantly worse outcome. All Orders Resolved
All outstanding compliance orders from previous inspections have been satisfactorily addressed and closed. The device returns to a clean compliance status. Our action: Update the device record. Close all open compliance orders in our tracking system. Confirm with
the building owner. Administrative Outcomes
Several outcomes in the TSSA system are administrative rather than inspection results.

When in doubt, treat the alteration as Minor A
and request the inspection. It is far better to schedule an unnecessary inspection than to skip a required one
and face enforcement action. Enforcement Action (ED-Enforcement Action)
An enforcement action inspection is an unannounced visit by a TSSA inspector, triggered by compliance
concerns. These carry significant operational and reputational implications. What Triggers an Enforcement Action
Enforcement actions may be triggered by: complaints from building occupants or the public, a pattern of
failed periodic inspections, intelligence from other regulatory sources, findings during inspections at the
same property, reports of unlicensed operation, or reports of devices in service that should be shut down. How They Work
We receive no advance notice. A TSSA inspector arrives at the building and requires immediate access. The
building owner is legally obligated to provide access. If our technician is not on-site (and they usually are not,
since these are unannounced), the inspector proceeds without one. The inspector has the authority to issue
immediate compliance orders or shut down the device on the spot. What to Do If an Enforcement Inspector Arrives
If a building owner or property manager contacts us to report an enforcement inspector:
1. Dispatch the nearest available technician immediately. 2. Instruct the building contact to provide full access. Do not delay or obstruct. 3. Notify the zone manager and Compliance and Regulatory Affairs. 4. If the technician arrives during the inspection, introduce themselves and cooperate fully. 5. Document the visit: inspector name, what was examined, orders issued, verbal instructions. Why Enforcement Actions Matter
A pattern of enforcement actions suggests systemic failures in our maintenance program. Compliance and
Regulatory Affairs reviews all enforcement actions quarterly. Zones showing a pattern require the zone
manager to present a corrective action plan. The ED-FU Enforcement Action Insp is the follow-up to verify that enforcement action issues have been
resolved. These follow-ups are tracked with the same priority as the original enforcement action. 8
Incident and Near-Miss Inspections
When an incident or near-miss is reported to the TSSA, they may dispatch an inspector to examine the device
and investigate. ED-Perform L1 Incident Insp
A Level 1 incident inspection is triggered by a reported incident involving injury, entrapment, or significant
equipment failure.

ED-Perform L1 Incident Insp
A Level 1 incident inspection is triggered by a reported incident involving injury, entrapment, or significant
equipment failure. The inspector:
• Examines the device in its current state (this is why preserving the scene is critical)
• Reviews maintenance records and the recent inspection history
• Interviews witnesses if present
• Determines the probable root cause of the incident
• May order the device shut down pending further investigation or repairs
ED-Perform L1 Near Miss Insp
A Level 1 near-miss inspection follows a reported event that could have resulted in injury but did not. The
same investigation process applies, though the urgency may be lower since no injury occurred. Near-miss
inspections are important because they often identify conditions that, if left unaddressed, would lead to an
actual incident. Our Role During Incident and Near-Miss Inspections
1. Preserve the scene. Do not reset, repair, or adjust anything until the TSSA inspector has examined it. If
passengers are trapped, follow the entrapment rescue procedure first, then preserve the scene. 2. Provide maintenance records. The inspector will want the device log book, recent service reports, the
last inspection report, and any open compliance orders. 3. Cooperate fully. Answer all questions honestly. Do not speculate about causes; report what is known. 4. Document everything. Record the timeline of events, who was notified, actions taken, and the inspector's
findings. These inspections feed into the TSSA's root cause classification system, which categorizes incidents by
contributing factors. Our internal data mirrors these categories (component failure, maintenance-related,
environmental, installation error, vandalism, or unknown) for our own risk analysis. Re-Activation Inspection (ED-Re-Activate Inspection)
A re-activation inspection is required before any shut-down device can return to service, whether the
shutdown was TSSA-initiated or voluntary (sometimes called a Customer Shutdown). Scope
The inspection scope depends on how long the device has been out of service:
• Under 6 months: inspector focuses on the shutdown reason and verifies it has been resolved, plus a
general safety assessment. 9
• 6 months to 1 year: expands to cover most of a periodic inspection, since idle components may have
deteriorated. • Over 1 year: essentially an initial inspection.

Our action: Update the device record. Close all open compliance orders in our tracking system. Confirm with
the building owner. Administrative Outcomes
Several outcomes in the TSSA system are administrative rather than inspection results. These include:
Cancelled (scheduled but cancelled, may need rescheduling), Dismantled (device removed, update records),
DC Follow up (Director's Compliance order follow-up), Extend Time to Comply (TSSA granted a deadline
extension), Order Transferred (orders moved to a different responsible party, e.g., after ownership change),
Received (TSSA received documentation, awaiting processing), RC Established (Responsible Contact
registered for the device), Temp Lic Not Needed (temporary license application deemed unnecessary), and
Complete / Inspection Complete (inspection process finished, final result recorded separately). Common Reasons for Failed Inspections
Based on our fleet experience, these are the most frequent reasons for failed periodic inspections. Door Interlock Issues
Door interlocks are the most frequently cited violation across our fleet. Common problems include worn
contacts that no longer make reliable connection, misadjusted rollers that allow the door to be opened slightly
12
with the car away from the landing, and bent or damaged assemblies from impact or vandalism. Door
interlocks should be checked during every routine maintenance visit, not just before inspections. Pit Conditions
Pit-related violations are the second most common category: water accumulation (sump pump failure,
drainage issues, groundwater), debris (construction materials, garbage, rodent activity), non-functional pit
stop switches, inadequate lighting, and unsecured pit ladders. Building owners sometimes use elevator pits
as unofficial storage. Our technicians should flag pit conditions during every visit and report them to the
building owner in writing. Machine Room Issues
Machine rooms are cited for storing materials unrelated to the elevator, inadequate ventilation or excessive
temperature, uncleaned oil leaks, insufficient lighting, and disconnect switches blocked by stored materials. Emergency Communication Failures
The emergency phone or intercom must connect to a monitored station at all times. Common failures: phone
line disconnected (building telecom changes, unpaid monitoring service), handset damaged or missing,
incorrect location information at the monitoring station, and non-functional TTY or accessibility
communication. Fire Service Test Records
Common violations: no record of Phase I and Phase II testing in the log book, expired testing records, and
incomplete records (only one phase tested).

scenarios.label: Follow-up needed list
scenarios.message: Which elevators need a followup inspection?
scenarios.reply:
A followup inspection is required when an inspector has issued compliance orders (deficiencies) during a previous inspection and needs to verify those issues have been resolved. The followup is scheduled to check that corrective action was taken — it isn't tied to a specific device type or risk level, but rather to the presence of outstanding orders.

If you're looking at a specific fleet or dashboard, you'd identify these elevators by finding devices whose most recent inspection outcome was "Fail" or "Follow up," indicating outstanding compliance work.

scenarios.label: RAG procedural — hydraulic
scenarios.message: What is the procedure for hydraulic pressure loss?
scenarios.reply:
## Procedure for Hydraulic Pressure Loss

Based on the maintenance documentation, hydraulic pressure loss is diagnosed through a series of pressure tests. Here's the procedure:

### Static Pressure Test
1. Connect a pressure gauge to the test port.
2. Allow the system to stabilize for at least 2 minutes after the car has stopped.
3. Record the static pressure reading.
4. Monitor the pressure for 5 minutes.
5. **Interpretation**: A stable reading indicates good seal integrity. A gradual drop indicates an internal leak, either at the cylinder seals or the control valve.

> **Note**: Normal static pressure varies by system design, but most passenger elevators in our fleet operate in the 200 to 500 psi range (14 to 35 bar). The system's design pressure is on the data plate.

### Running Pressure Test
This measures system pressure while the car travels upward under load:
1. With the gauge still connected, send the car on a full up-run under load.
2. Record the peak pressure during the run.
3. Compare to the rated working pressure on the data plate.
4. Running pressure should be within 10% of the rated working pressure.

> **Interpretation**: Pressure significantly below rated may indicate a worn pump, internal valve bypass, or low fluid. Pressure significantly above rated may indicate a restriction in the hydraulic line or an improperly adjusted relief valve.

### If Pressure Loss is Confirmed
- **Leaking valve**: The valve does not seat fully, allowing fluid to bypass. This is the most common valve failure and a frequent source of leveling complaints.
- **Solenoid failure**: The electrical solenoid that actuates the valve burns out or loses its magnetic strength.

All hydraulic repairs beyond basic monitoring require a contractor (typically KONE for our fleet). If you encounter pressure loss during testing, document the findings and escalate to the appropriate contractor.

**Source**: Maintenance Document 10078

scenarios.label: RAG procedural — cable replacement
scenarios.message: What maintenance is required after a cable replacement?
scenarios.reply:
After a cable replacement on an elevating device in Ontario, the TSSA requires a **Re-Inspection (Re-Activation)** before the device can return to service. This is because cable replacement is classified as a **Minor A alteration** — a replacement in kind of a safety-critical component.

During the re-activation inspection, the TSSA inspector will verify:

- Proper cable tension and equalization between multiple cables
- Correct routing and alignment over sheaves and in grooves
- Secure anchorage and termination points
- That governor cables (if applicable) are properly adjusted
- Functional testing of related safety devices (e.g., overspeed governor, brake system)

The device cannot operate legally until a licensed inspector has examined the work and cleared it. The inspection outcome is recorded as Passed, Failed, or Follow up depending on findings.

For ongoing maintenance after the replacement, the contractor should include cable condition in their routine inspections — checking for wear, corrosion, or improper tension at each periodic service visit. Any signs of cable damage or misalignment should be addressed promptly to prevent premature replacement.

If you need the specific regulatory citation, this falls under the alteration definitions in **O. Reg. 209/01** and the TSSA's alteration inspection policies. For compliance questions about a specific device, direct inquiries to the TSSA or a licensed elevator contractor.

scenarios.label: Definition — TSSA acronym
scenarios.message: What does TSSA stand for?
scenarios.reply: TSSA stands for the **Technical Standards and Safety Authority**, the provincial administrative authority that regulates elevating devices (including elevators), boilers, pressure vessels, and other technical systems in Ontario. It operates under the *Technical Standards and Safety Act* and administers O. Reg. 209/01 — Elevating Devices, which sets out the licensing, inspection, and safety requirements for elevators in the province.

scenarios.label: Definition — Customer Shutdown
scenarios.message: What is a Customer Shutdown?
scenarios.reply:
A **Customer Shutdown** is a voluntary, building-owner-initiated status where an elevator is taken out of service. The device remains mechanically intact — it's not a regulatory action. Common reasons include prolonged vacancy, renovation, or planned seasonal closure.

Because the elevator has been out of service, it requires a **Re-Activation Inspection** before it can legally return to service. This ensures the device is still safe to operate after the shutdown period.

This differs from a **TSSA Shutdown**, which is an enforcement order issued by the regulator and carries higher compliance priority.
